query: Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a simple solid-solution state has favorable plasticity and machinability but relatively low hardness and strength, while its deformation behavior remains poorly understood. Under mechanical-property and deformation testing, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs this low hardness and strength and why? Define a controlled comparison, predict the observations relative to the starting state, state the applicable composition, structural-state, and loading boundaries, connect the hypothesis to the reported property combination, and specify a falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: The low hardness and strength of equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a simple solid-solution state result from the absence of effective microstructural obstacles—such as a refined grain structure or strengthening precipitates—that would normally impede dislocation motion. In this state, deformation is dominated by facile grain-boundary-mediated plasticity and unimpeded dislocation flow, which explains the excellent plasticity and machinability but low resistance to deformation.
generation.material_initial_state: Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi processed into a single-phase solid solution with relatively coarse grains and no secondary phases or precipitate strengthening features.
generation.intervention: Apply a thermo-mechanical treatment to refine the grain size and/or trigger the controlled formation of fine precipitates while maintaining overall equimolar composition.
generation.conditions: Mechanical tests (e.g., nanoindentation, uniaxial tension or compression) performed at ambient temperature and under quasi-static loading conditions; composition retained as equimolar CoCrFeNiTi.
generation.structural_mediator: The grain boundaries and (if introduced) the fine precipitates that serve as obstacles to dislocation motion.
generation.mechanism: In the as-produced state the homogeneous solid solution lacks significant lattice barriers (such as high lattice distortion or precipitate pinning), so dislocations can move easily and grain-boundary sliding becomes dominant. This mechanism yields lower hardness and yield strength, while still permitting plastic deformation and good machinability. Refining the grain structure or introducing precipitates is expected to hinder dislocation and grain-boundary movement, thereby enhancing strength and hardness.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline alloy, the thermo-mechanically processed alloy with a refined grain structure (and possible fine precipitates) will exhibit a measurable increase in hardness and yield strength, as indicated by higher nanoindentation hardness values and a shifted deformation mode from grain-boundary sliding to more dislocation pile-up or controlled dislocation motion.
generation.baseline: The original equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a simple coarse-grained solid-solution state that shows favorable plasticity and machinability with relatively low hardness and strength.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is applicable to equimolar high-entropy alloys in simple solid solution states tested at room temperature under quasi-static loading. It may not apply under high strain rate, extreme temperature conditions, or if secondary phases are already present.
generation.uncertainty: The relative contributions of grain-boundary sliding versus dislocation-mediated deformation, and the exact quantitative improvement expected from grain refinement or precipitate formation, remain uncertain until further microstructural characterization (e.g., grain size distribution, precipitate identification) and in situ deformation analyses are conducted.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of equimolar CoCrFeNiTi samples: one in the untreated (coarse-grained simple solid solution) condition and another that has undergone thermo-mechanical processing to achieve significant grain refinement and/or controlled precipitate formation. Subject both sets to nanoindentation and uniaxial mechanical tests (tension/compression) at ambient temperature.
measurements: Dislocation density and deformation mechanism analysis via TEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the processed samples do not show a significant increase (e.g., an increase of at least 20% in hardness and yield strength) or if microstructural analysis does not reveal a shift from grain-boundary sliding to a dislocation-impeded mechanism compared to the baseline, then the hypothesis that the lack of microstructural obstacles governs the low hardness and strength is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Paper card. Question: How can a nanocrystalline refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) film with superior mechanical and tribological properties be synthesized using a cost-effective single target, and what are the effects of annealing on its adhesion and wear performance?. System: Equimolar CuMoTaWV refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) film deposited on silicon and 304 stainless-steel substrates. Processing: DC-magnetron sputtering using a single target prepared by partial spark plasma sintering (SPS) of equimolar elemental powders (Cu, Mo, Ta, W, V) at 1000 °C under 40 MPa pressure; film deposition at 500 °C substrate temperature for 120 min in Ar atmosphere (1.16 × 10⁻³ mPa, 150 W power); post-deposition annealing at 300 °C for adhesion improvement. Test conditions: Nanoindentation at 3 mN load; nanopillar compression (440 nm diameter, 3 mN max force); tribological wear tests at room temperature (RT) and 300 °C with 1 N load and 0.1 m/s sliding speed against E52100 alloy steel counterballs. Findings: The as-deposited film exhibited a nanocrystalline body-centered cubic (BCC) solid solution with an average grain size of 18 nm and a thickness of ~900 nm.; Nanoindentation measurement
